sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** Answer: no.
   - **Where:** There is no main image. All content sits in a column from x≈160 to 790, and the right side from x≈800 to 1280 is empty white for the full height. Below the button (y≈570–800) is empty too.
   - **What the viewer gets:** A promise of a "calm" crossing and watching "the harbour slide past from the open deck," with nothing to see. The headline has to do all the persuading alone. The lopsided empty right half makes the section look unfinished, as if a picture failed to load. Without a picture of the bay, the boat or the deck, this could be any service's page in the same blue: nothing shows this crossing.
   - **Why:** This is common sense and taste. The catalog entry's sources are not on the approved list. The copy sells an experience you look at, and a picture is the cheapest way to make it believable.
   - **Fix:** If an image was meant to fill the right half, check that it loads, and then this line becomes yes. If not, add one that finishes the headline instead of illustrating it. For example, the view from the open deck mid-crossing would show the "calm" the headline only claims, rather than a stock photo of a ferry. If the page is meant to be text-only, rebalance the layout so the emptiness looks chosen rather than vacant.
   - **Type and weight:** Defect if the image is missing, taste otherwise. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- The purpose is clear in one read. The eyebrow names the company, the headline gives a concrete benefit with a number ("twelve calm minutes"), and the button names one exact next step ("See the timetable"). A stranger knows what this is and what to do within seconds.
- It hangs together as one thing. The only colour is a single blue, shared by the "Coastal Ferry Co." eyebrow and the button. There is one typeface, generous calm spacing, and no ornament. Nothing on the page is extra, and the restraint suits the word "calm".

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (main image and headline make one idea)

**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
1. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** Answer: no. The paragraph (about x 160–785, y 270–355) looks about 20 px. The three feature lines below it (about y 388–475) look about 18 px. Both are the same typeface and regular weight, in the same dark ink. The list has no bullets, icons or extra spacing to mark it as a list. So the viewer sees the paragraph and then a slightly smaller paragraph, and can't tell whether the feature lines are a new level (the quick points to scan) or just more body text that happens to be a touch smaller. That makes the size step look like an accident rather than a choice. Sizes this close don't read as separate levels (Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, 3.1.1 "Don't compose without a scale"). A small difference in one kind of contrast reads as a mistake (Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8). Fix: set the list at the paragraph's size, or decide it is its own level and mark that in a way you can see at a glance, such as bullets or icons, a different weight or colour, or laying the three points side by side. Don't rely on a one-step size change. Kind: convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The headline clearly leads. At about 52 px bold, against about 20 px regular body text, it is roughly 2.5 times the size and much heavier. The eye lands there first, and the promise ("twelve calm minutes") is the first thing read.
- The levels differ in more than size. The eyebrow "Coastal Ferry Co." is small but bold and brand blue, so it reads as a label, not as body text. The button repeats that blue as a solid shape, which makes it a clear second stop after the headline. Colour does the work, so no extra size is needed.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (each level of the text distinct, with no two sizes almost the same)

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **The empty space isn't gathered into deliberate areas, and the visual weight doesn't balance** (two checklist lines, one problem). Every element sits in a column from x 160 to about x 790, between y 90 and y 568. The right side, about 480 × 800 px (x 800–1280), is empty, and so is the band below the button (y 570–800). Nothing is on the right to balance the headline and the blue button on the left.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** The frame looks like it's tipping to the upper left, and the empty right side looks like a picture failed to load. It doesn't read as space left open on purpose. The piece looks unfinished, and a ferry company loses the one thing a ferry hero usually sells: the bay and the boat.
   - **Why:** Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, "Balance": a heavy side needs a counterweight. Tschichold and Müller-Brockmann: large empty areas with no explanation are a fault. White space should be shaped and given a size on purpose, not left over.
   - **If it's a capture problem:** If a picture belongs on the right and didn't load, check the live page. The finding then becomes making sure it always loads, with a fallback.
   - **Fix:** Either fill the right column with a counterweight (a photo of the deck or the crossing, or the next departure time as a large figure), or make the emptiness clearly intended. For the second option, scale the type and column up, or pull the block toward the optical centre, so the empty area has a size and shape of its own.
   - Defect. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- **Grouping by space.** The small eyebrow sits tight above the headline. The blocks are separated by even gaps of about 40 px, and the three feature lines sit closer together than the gap to the paragraph. The groups read correctly without rules or boxes.
- **One left edge.** The eyebrow, headline, paragraph, list and button all start exactly at x 160, which gives a clean reading path from the headline down to the button.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the empty right half is a picture that didn't load, and how the column reflows on narrower screens. Check both in a live browser.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (white space gathered and deliberate; visual weight balances)

**Section.** Text: applies. The image is one landing-page hero with an eyebrow, a two-line headline, a paragraph, a three-item list and a button.

**Findings**
1. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name?** No. The headline (about x 160–750, y 130–240) breaks as "Cross the bay in twelve / calm minutes". The one fact the headline is selling, "twelve minutes", is split across the line end. The reader meets "twelve" with nothing after it, then has to join it to "minutes" on the next line, with "calm" in between. The first line also ends on a dangling number, so the promise lands a beat late. The direction of the fix is to keep "twelve calm minutes" together on the second line ("Cross the bay in / twelve calm minutes"). A non-breaking space between "twelve" and "calm", or a slightly narrower headline box, would do it, and the two lines would also come out closer in length. This is a convention (it is the checklist's line-break rule). I could not open the catalog entry because the entries script was refused, so the source behind it isn't checked. Weight: minor.

2. **Not a checklist line, from reading the copy:** the paragraph says boats run "every forty minutes from early morning until late evening" (y ≈ 282–313). The viewer will plan around those times, and "early morning" and "late evening" can be read many ways: a 6 am commuter and a 9 am day-tripper will each assume their own hour. That vagueness is a defect. The fix is to give the first and last sailing ("every 40 minutes, 6:20 am to 10:40 pm"), or to say outright that the times are in the timetable behind the button. Weight: minor, because the button leads to the timetable anyway.

**What's working.**
- The type is plain and well behaved. It uses one sans family in a few clearly separate steps: a small bold blue eyebrow, a heavy headline of about 56 px with tight leading so its two lines hold together, and body text of about 18 px. The paragraph runs about 65–70 characters a line with generous leading and an easy rag. Keep this scale and measure when revising.
- The three list items are single short lines in sentence case on a crisp left edge, so they read in one pass without bullets.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** I couldn't check how the headline break and the 65–70 character measure hold up at other widths. The break in particular may move or get worse on mobile, so check it at narrow widths in a browser.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (headings break at phrase boundaries, not between a number and its unit)

I worked from the full image (1280×800, about one screen) because the crop and entries scripts were refused. No measurements were taken; all sizes and character counts are estimates by eye.

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes).** First read: the eye lands on the black headline, drops through the grey-black body, and stops on the blue "See the timetable" button. It reads as a calm, plain landing hero for a local ferry, aimed at day-trippers. It feels clean and restrained but a little bloodless. Color:
- Small palette: yes (white, near-black text, one mid-dark blue)
- Saturated color a small share: yes (blue only on the eyebrow at 160,100 and the button at 160–369 × 513–568)
- Value range holds in grayscale: yes (near-black on white; the button fill is dark enough to hold its shape)
- Warm forward, cool recede: yes (no warm color; the CTA comes forward on fill and value, which serves the piece)
- Matching colors look the same: yes (eyebrow blue and button blue read as one)
- No vibrating edges: yes (white on dark blue)
- Status colors used for their meaning: yes (blue as brand or action is its usual meaning)
- Color never carries meaning alone: yes (the button has a shape and a label, and the eyebrow is plain text)
- Dark theme background: yes (not a dark theme)

No line answered no or unsure, so I opened no entries.

---

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One accent color, used twice and nowhere else.** The same blue marks the brand name ("Coastal Ferry Co.", top left at about 160,100) and the one action ("See the timetable", 160–369 × 513–568). The page's only saturated fill sits on its only action, so the eye ends on the button without any help from size. Keep the blue to those two places. A third use, such as blue bullets on the three feature lines, would dilute it.
- **The page holds up in grayscale.** Near-black headline and body on white, with a dark blue button, keep the order of reading (headline, then copy, then button) even with the color taken out. The hierarchy rests on value, not hue, so it survives color-vision deficiency and poor screens.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image has no photo, illustration, icon or logo mark. "Coastal Ferry Co." at about (160, 100) is set as plain blue text, not a drawn mark. The right half of the frame, from about x 800 to 1280, is empty white. If a hero image was meant to go there, the screenshot can't show whether it failed to load or was never designed. Check that in a live browser.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has one control, the "See the timetable" button.

**Findings**
1. **Do the navigation and components follow the conventions users know from the platform and similar products? / Do the grouping, names, and navigation show how the product's parts relate?** The page has no header or navigation at all. The only sign of the operator is the small blue "Coastal Ferry Co." eyebrow at about 160,100, and it looks like a label, not a home link. There are no links to fares, routes, the other landing, tickets, or contact. A visitor who wants anything other than the timetable has no route to it, and can't tell what else the site holds or whether this is the home page. Transport sites always put the logo and main links across the top. Leaving them out gains nothing here and costs every visitor whose question isn't "when". Fix: add a standard top bar with the logo as a home link on the left and the few things riders need (Timetable, Fares, Getting to the landings, Contact) on the right, with the current page marked. The empty right half of the page has room for it. Convention (Nielsen, Jakob's law; Norman, *The Design of Everyday Things*, ch. 2, conceptual model). Weight: major.
2. **Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them instead of making them hunt for it?** This is the body paragraph at about 160,270–355 and the button at 160,513. A rider comes for the next boat time and the fare. The page gives "every forty minutes from early morning until late evening", which can't be planned around: what time is "early", and at what minute past the hour? The real times are one click away. Fix: show the next two or three departures from the north landing (or first and last boat plus the minutes past the hour), and the fare, right on the page, and keep the button for the full timetable. The ask then stops being "go look" and lets the rider judge the trip straight away. Taste / common sense; the catalog source for this line isn't on the approved list. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- There is exactly one action, and it can't be missed. The solid blue button at 160,513 is the only filled shape on the page, and it is about 209×55 px, well above any target minimum.
- The label says exactly where it goes. "See the timetable" names the destination, not a vague "Learn more", so link purpose is clear from the text alone.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the button shows a visible focus ring (2 px, 3:1) when reached by keyboard. Check this in a live browser, because the button is the page's only action.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 29 yes, 3 no (navigation follows conventions; navigation shows how parts relate; puts what the user needs next in front of them), 1 unsure (focus indicator)
